title: Who was Dorothy Parker, really?
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Dorothy Parker, the witty poet, short story writer, critic and screenwriter of the 1920s through 1960s. They cover her childhood and early tragedies, her start at Vanity Fair and Vogue and her firing over a review, her membership in the Algonquin Round Table, her poetry and short fiction, her Hollywood screenwriting with Alan Campbell, her left-wing activism and blacklisting, and her death, unusual ashes story, and Woodlawn burial. The episode closes with a listener mail about PBIS (positive behavioral interventions and supports) in schools.

segments.title: Opening banter and why Dorothy Parker
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the jazz age and a Dorothy Parker movie, then introduce her as a very witty writer remembered more for her wit than her large body of work, and note the difficulty of explaining why she matters.

segments.title: Early life and family tragedies
segments.summary: Parker is born Dorothy Rothschild in New Jersey and raised on the Upper West Side. Her mother dies when she is four, her father and stepmother are described as harsh, and her father dies after her uncle's poor investments leave little money. Her first job is playing piano at a dance school.

segments.title: Vanity Fair, Vogue, and the drama critic role
segments.summary: Parker sells her first poem to Vanity Fair in 1914 for twelve dollars. Frank Crowninshield hires her at Vogue for ten dollars a week, where she writes captions and slips in jokes. She becomes Vanity Fair's drama critic at age 24, known for backhanded compliments and cutting remarks about high society.

segments.title: Firing from Vanity Fair and her critical style
segments.summary: Parker is fired in 1920 after a review that insulted an actress tied to an influential advertiser's wife. Benchley and Sherwood quit in protest. The hosts discuss her subjective, untrained criticism, her occasional praise, and her famous one-liners.

segments.title: The Algonquin Round Table
segments.summary: The Round Table began with a June 1919 lunch welcoming back Alexander Woollcott, and became a long-running gathering of writers, actors and columnists at the Algonquin Hotel. Members collaborated and used each other as characters. Parker later downplayed the group, and the hosts discuss its fame and her distance from it.

segments.title: Famous quotes and the Esquire profile
segments.summary: The hosts share famous Parker quotes, including the Calvin Coolidge death quip and the horticulture line, and note misattributed quotes she denied. They recommend Wyatt Cooper's Esquire profile of her.

segments.title: Freelance career, poetry, and self-doubt
segments.summary: After leaving Vanity Fair, Parker freelances for magazines and writes for The New Yorker. She publishes poetry books and short story collections, including the bestselling Enough! and an O. Henry prize story. She later stops writing poetry, and the hosts discuss her self-doubt and her preference for isolation.

segments.title: Hollywood screenwriting, Alan Campbell, and blacklisting
segments.summary: Parker moves to Hollywood and writes screenplays with her husband Alan Campbell, who dies later; she is credited on A Star Is Born. Her left-wing activism, anti-Nazi stance, and Scottsboro Boys fundraising lead to her being placed on Red Channels and blacklisted, and she testifies before HUAC in 1955 and takes the Fifth.

segments.title: Final years, will dispute, ashes, and burial
segments.summary: Parker returns to New York and leaves her estate to Martin Luther King Jr. and then the NAACP. Her friend Lillian Hellman, named executor, is angry at being left out and discards papers, and a memorial goes against Parker's wish for a quiet cremation. Her ashes sit in a lawyer's desk drawer from 1973 until they are moved to Woodlawn Cemetery with the epitaph 'Excuse my dust.'

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the Dorothy Parker episode and recommend the HowStuffWorks article on her.

segments.title: Listener mail on PBIS
segments.summary: Listener Jennifer writes as a former teacher criticizing positive behavioral interventions and supports (PBIS) in schools, which the hosts had discussed in an earlier listener mail. Josh invites counterpoints.
